details:
**This Is Just To Say** – a short, apologetic poem in which the speaker confesses to eating plums “that were in the icebox” and describes them as “so sweet / and so cold.” The poem’s fame makes it a signature clue for Williams.  

**The Red Wheelbarrow** – a four‑line poem consisting of two short couplets that famously begins “so much depends / upon … a red wheelbarrow,” illustrating Williams’s imagist focus on ordinary objects.  

**Paterson** – a multi‑volume modern epic about the city of Paterson, New Jersey, in which Williams repeatedly declares “no ideas but in things,” a central tenet of his poetic philosophy.  

**“no ideas but in things”** – the concise dictum Williams used to define his imagist approach, appearing in the preface to Paterson and often quoted in scholarship.  

**Imagist poet who invented the triadic line** – Williams created the three‑line stanza (often 3‑5‑3 syllables) that structures many of his poems, a distinctive formal hallmark.  

**Asphodel, That Greeny Flower** – a poem in which the speaker repeats “I come, my sweet, to sing to you,” addressing his wife; the title’s unusual spelling (“Greeny”) is a memorable identifier.  

**Danse Russe** – a poem containing the self‑referential line “Who shall say I am not / the happy genius of my household?” which is frequently cited in quizbowl as a Williams clue.  

**Spring and All** – a collection opening with the line “By the road to the contagious hospital,” noted for its surreal opening and for introducing the “greeny flower” motif.  

**Pictures from Brueghel** – a later poetry collection whose title references the Flemish painter Brueghel; it contains the “splash unnoticed” image and other vivid visual poems.  

**The Great Figure / I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold** – a poem describing a numeral 5 seen on a fire engine, which inspired Charles Demuth’s famous painting of the same title.  

**Flossie (Flossie Stecher) wrote the “Reply”** – Williams’s wife responded to “This Is Just To Say” with a brief “Reply” that begins “Please shut off the telephone,” linking the personal anecdote to the poet.  

**Physician at Passaic (General) Hospital** – Williams practiced medicine in the Passaic area while composing Paterson, a biographical detail that frequently appears in clues.  

**Triadic line form (3‑5‑3 syllable pattern)** – the structural pattern Williams used in poems like “Asphodel, That Greeny Flower” and “Danse Russe,” distinguishing his style from other modernists.
